rationale: The book defines 'heart of the earth' as Jerusalem, identifying it as the navel and heart of the land. This is supported by Ezekiel 5:5 and 38:12, which place Jerusalem in the 'midst of the nations' and the 'midst of the land' (where the Greek word for earth, gē, also translates to land). The linguistic parallelism with Jonah being cast into the 'heart of the seas' (Jonah 2:3) strongly corroborates reading 'heart' as center or midst and 'earth' as land. This lexical and geographic linkage provides a scripturally defined referent, whereas the traditional view requires treating 'heart of the earth' as an isolated idiom for the grave or Hades, which no other scripture uses.
book_core_identification: 'Heart of the earth' refers to Jerusalem, functioning as the center or midst of the land.
book_secondary_elaborations: the navel and heart of the land
chapter_only_objections: The claim that the three days and three nights begin precisely at Jesus' arrest on Thursday night may face chronological and textual scrutiny regarding the harmony of the passion week.
The identification of the 'great fish' specifically as Caesar/Rome acting through Jerusalem, rather than a generic vehicle of death/judgment, is an elaborate typological mapping.
The equation of Jonah's 'ship' to the covenant polity of Jerusalem is a complex allegorical reading that goes beyond the glossary definition.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The 'heart of the earth' means the grave or Sheol/Hades (the underworld), paralleling Jonah's time in the 'belly of Sheol' (Jonah 2:2) as a direct reference to Jesus' death and burial.
counter_core_identification: The grave or subterranean underworld realm of the dead.
material_core_denial: The phrase refers to the physical or spiritual realm of the dead, not a geographic or political city (Jerusalem) on the surface of the land.
counter_case: Jonah 2:2 explicitly identifies his location in the fish as the 'belly of Sheol', a standard Old Testament term for the realm of the dead, strongly linking the 'heart of the earth' to the underworld.
The sign of Jonah is overwhelmingly associated with Jesus' death and resurrection; the three days and nights apply most naturally to his time dead in the tomb.
Ephesians 4:9 refers to Jesus descending to the 'lower parts of the earth', providing a close conceptual parallel to the 'heart of the earth' as a subterranean realm.
book_explanatory_advantages: Directly maps 'heart' to 'midst' and 'earth' to 'land' using Ezekiel 5:5 and 38:12, giving the phrase a scripturally attested referent.
Maintains structural and linguistic parallelism with Jonah's destination in the 'heart of the seas' (Jonah 2:3).

Resolves the chronological difficulty of fitting 'three days and three nights' into the traditional Friday-to-Sunday burial timeline by starting the count at his delivery into the custody of Jerusalem.
Avoids reading a unique, standalone idiom for the grave ('heart of the earth') into Matthew 12:40 when Scripture never calls a tomb the heart of the earth.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Explains the 'belly of Sheol' language in Jonah 2:2 by directly equating the fish's belly to the state of death.
Focuses the fulfillment strictly on the death and resurrection event without needing to extend the period backward to include the arrest and trials.
